Hong Kong, China; Macao, China; and Taiwan, China: Separate Trademark Registrations

The most common misconception about Chinese trademark protection is geographical. A CNIPA registration covers the Chinese mainland only. All three of Hong Kong, China; Macao, China; and Taiwan, China are parts of China, but each has its own trademark registry and requires a separate local filing.

Separate Trademark Registries Within China

The single most common misconception about Chinese trademark protection is geographical. A registration granted by CNIPA is effective in the Chinese mainland only. It does not automatically protect the brand in Hong Kong, China; Macao, China; or Taiwan, China.

All three are parts of China, but each maintains its own trademark system, its own registry and its own examination practice, and each requires a separate application to its local authority. Rights are therefore territorial within China in a very practical sense: to be protected in all of these markets, a brand has to obtain protection in each of them. This is a procedural feature of how trademark rights are obtained locally, nothing more.

The consequence is easy to state and easy to overlook in a budget. A portfolio built only around a CNIPA registration can leave the brand unprotected in markets where the goods are actually sold, distributed or advertised. Conversely, a registration obtained in one of the three regions gives no rights in the Chinese mainland. Plan the map first, then file.

What a CNIPA Registration Covers

The coverage rules are symmetrical: a registration protects only in the place that granted it.

Registration obtainedWhere it is effectiveWhat it does not cover
CNIPA registrationThe Chinese mainlandHong Kong, China; Macao, China; and Taiwan, China
A registration in Hong Kong, ChinaThat regionThe Chinese mainland and the other two regions
A registration in Macao, ChinaThat regionThe Chinese mainland and the other two regions
A registration in Taiwan, ChinaThat regionThe Chinese mainland and the other two regions

Two practical points follow. First, a squatter can file in a market where you have no registration, and a CNIPA certificate will not by itself defeat that filing. Second, use evidence, licences and enforcement records have to be organised per registry, because genuine use in one place is not automatically use in another. Keep a separate file for each.

Why a Madrid Designation Does Not Extend

An international registration under the Madrid System that designates China is examined by CNIPA and, if accepted, produces protection in the Chinese mainland. It does not extend to Hong Kong, China; Macao, China; or Taiwan, China. Each of the three requires its own local application; a Madrid designation is not a substitute.

This trips up portfolios that were built centrally. A brand may hold a single international registration and assume its coverage is complete, only to find that the three local registers are untouched. When you audit an international portfolio, list the designated contracting party and then, separately, the local filings actually obtained in each of the three markets.

The same logic applies to watch services and renewal diaries: an alert configured only around CNIPA publications will not report filings in the three local registers. See Madrid versus direct filing for the broader route comparison.

Planning the Separate Filings

Because each registry is separate, plan a separate filing for each market where the brand is used or likely to be used. Applications are made to the respective local authorities under their own procedures, with their own formalities, language requirements and classification practice. Do not assume a specification accepted by CNIPA will be accepted unchanged elsewhere; have local counsel adapt the goods and services to the local table.

Sequence the filings around commercial exposure: the markets where goods are sold, where distributors operate, where e-commerce listings appear and where counterfeits are likely to originate. Where a launch is staged, file ahead of disclosure in each market, since a first-to-file system rewards the party that applies first. Keep the Latin mark and the Chinese-character mark as separate applications in every registry, and decide per market whether a device mark is needed.

We do not quote filing costs, official fees or processing times here: these vary by registry, by class and by the current fee schedules, and should be confirmed against the official announcements and rules in force at the time of filing. Ask local counsel for a current estimate for each market rather than applying a single figure across the portfolio.

A Coordinated Portfolio Checklist

A coordinated portfolio is more than four certificates. Use this checklist:

  1. Map the markets. Record, for each of the four registries, which classes, which marks and which local entity hold the rights.
  2. File Latin and Chinese-character names separately in each registry; they are separate rights.
  3. Keep use evidence per registry: dated sales, invoices, advertising and platform records that satisfy local requirements.
  4. Document licences and distributor relationships so that use by a local partner can be proved where needed.
  5. Extend watch and renewal calendars to the three local registers, not just CNIPA publications.
  6. Audit annually. Check owner names, addresses and class coverage, because a portfolio that drifts out of date is hard to enforce.

One brand, four registers. For the underlying filing mechanics see our China trademark registration guide and first-to-file guide; then add the three local applications as separate workstreams.

Sources and Caveats

Basis: the territorial scope of CNIPA registrations, which are effective in the Chinese mainland only; the separate trademark systems of Hong Kong, China; Macao, China; and Taiwan, China, each requiring applications to its own local authority; the absence of automatic reciprocal protection between the Chinese mainland and the three regions; and the rule that a Madrid designation of China does not extend to the three regions. All three are parts of China. Filing formalities, fees and practice are set by each local authority and may change, so confirm the current official announcements and rules before filing. This is general information, not legal advice.
